- If sentiment is strongly bullish (≥ 0.67) in recent days, model tends to overestimate prices; reduce forecast slope or cap upward momentum.
- If sentiment is bearish (≤ 0.33) and prices are trending down, model often underestimates the drop; adjust downward with steeper slope or add volatility buffer.
- After sharp price spikes (e.g., >10% from prior day), model frequently overshoots; apply a “cool-down” correction to prevent overreaction.
- When sentiment shifts from bullish to bearish (or vice versa), model lags in adjusting; add a 1–2 day lag correction or use sentiment as a trigger for re-calibration.
- In low-sentiment periods (sentiment ≤ 0.33 for 3+ consecutive days), model often underestimates mean reversion; increase forecast volatility or add a downward bias to reflect mean-reversion tendency.
- If model forecast is flat or rising slowly but true outcome shows strong divergence, sentiment may be misleading; use sentiment as a signal to adjust for “noise” or “market fatigue”.
- For 30-day forecasts, model often fails to capture short-term volatility spikes; consider adding a “volatility filter” or “sentiment-adjusted volatility multiplier” to forecast.
